title: Most Brits Oppose Tourist Taxes — Except in Hotspots
paragraphs: A number of cities around the world have tourist taxes — usually an extra charge added to the cost of accommodation.

These taxes might be used to help locals by putting money into things like buses or protecting the local environment. They can also be used to reduce tourist numbers — although if those numbers are reduced too much, that can also be a problem.
In England, the government said in September that it plans to let local mayors set and charge new tourist taxes. And while some people are happy with the idea, others are not.
A YouGov survey of nearly 60,000 adults in England, Wales and Scotland has found that 51% are against tourist taxes in their area, with just 37% saying they support them.
However, these results change for people living in some of Great Britain's tourist hotspots.

For example, 67% of survey participants in Scotland's capital, Edinburgh, say they would support a tourist tax. There are around 500,000 people living in Edinburgh, but the city welcomed 5 million overnight visitors in 2024.
And in Cornwall, 61% say they'd support a tourist tax. Cornwall is a popular seaside destination in the south of England that welcomed a record 5 million tourists in 2022.

However, that number fell by about 10%-15% in 2023, and again by about 10% in 2024. One of the main reasons for this decrease has been price, with Cornwall being one of the UK's more expensive places to stay.
But that decrease in visitors is also causing problems for hotels and other Cornish businesses that need tourists.

And not all tourist hotspots are sure they like the idea of a tax. In London, which got over 20 million international visitors in 2024, residents are split. Forty-two percent said they support a tax, while 44% are against it.
